title: Incantato
full_review:
Those wishing for a good wallow in a lush, old-fashioned, ostensibly romantic period piece may find what they're looking for in "Incantato" ("Enchanted") (Northern Arts Entertainment), but this stately paced, wildly improbable tale is pretty hard to swallow.

The time is the 1920s, and the place Bologna, Italy. Nello (Neri Marcore), a painfully shy 35-year-old classics professor whose father, Cesare (Giancarlo Giannini), serves as tailor to the pope, has relocated to that city to teach high school. So pure is he that his father checks out whether his new roommate, a barber, at the boarding house where he'll reside, is an "invert." (He isn't.)

In short order, the distinctly straight roommate -- who thinks nothing of making out with his girlfriend in the room under Nello's nose -- suggests that the girl's sister would be a perfect match for the inexperienced Nello, who's never had a girlfriend. Just one catch: she's blind.

So, at a Sunday tea dance, where the blind girls -- all distinctly plain, to put it mildly -- get to cut a prim rug with the male visitors, Nello is introduced to the exceedingly homely sister. When he politely excuses himself and flees to another room, Angela (Vanessa Incontrada), a stunning young blind woman, enters from the garden and steals his heart, particularly when it turns out she knows the classics. (This is the feature film debut of model and television presenter Incontrada, whom director Pupi Avati discovered in an ad for cell phones, and she looks far too contemporary in this period setting.)

Angela's disapproving father warns Nello that his daughter is a hopeless flirt and that his heart will be broken but, undeterred, Nello pursues the romance, and Angela succumbs, though it's clear she still carries a torch for her ex-boyfriend, Guido, who dumped her after she lost her sight. She attempts to shame her ex by ostentatiously going up to a "private room" above a restaurant with Nello, while the diners -- including Guido -- look on, aghast.

Later, sensing Nello's naivete, she sleeps with him and agrees to marry him.

Nello invites his parents to meet her, and rather than warmly embracing the girl, considering she's more of a knockout than they might ever have imagined for the doltish Nello, they react as if Angela had leprosy, the mother stifling prodigious tears, though Cesare eventually gives his tacit approval.

Whether the two live happily ever after and whether Angela regains her sight are two developments we shan't spoil, but, suffice to say, the film calls for major suspension of disbelief. Avati calls this a "fable," as well he should, as it is amusingly unbelievable, from the adoring students who are unaccountably smitten with their sweet but dopey teacher, to Angela's well-to-do father sending his newly blinded daughter to what looks like a Dickensian asylum.

Though Marcore, known in Italy as a comic and an impersonator, has a certain puppy-dog vulnerability, and Incontrada looks fetching with or without her dark shades, there isn't much chemistry between them, even if they make an interesting study in contrasts.

The final scenes of the film take place in the Vatican with Cesare delivering his wares, as Nello assists. There's a touching scene meant to evoke Charlie Chaplin's "City Lights," but it's too little, too late.

The period trappings are lovely, and the movie does recall an era of Italian films of Vittorio DeSica, Ettore Scola and Dino Risi. Riz Ortolani has composed a lush score evocative of the films of yore. But Avati's film moves at a lugubrious pace. Give Avati credit for trying to say something about handicaps -- both physical and emotional -- and also for paying homage to the romanticism of the past.

The portrayal of Cesare's duties for the pope are unobjectionable (though Cesare himself is presented as a womanizer), and the church elements are dealt with in respectful fashion. Cesare even has a long speech about the thrill of dressing the pope.

"Incantato" allegedly received the longest ovation at the 2003 Cannes Film Festival of any film up to that point, a fact that may set you wondering what they're putting in the water there.

Subtitles.

Because of some mild sexual episodes and rear nudity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
